title: Κιθαρῳδός
part: The Singer to the Lyre (Chambry 156 · Perry 121)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 156 (= Perry 121). Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Κιθαρῳδὸς ἀφυὴς ἐν κεκονιαμένῳ οἴκῳ συνεχῶς ᾄδων, ἀντηχούσης αὐτῷ τῆς φωνῆς, ἐνόμισεν αὐτὸν εὔφωνον σφόδρα εἶναι.
sentences.tr: Kitharōidos aphyēs en kekoniamenōi oikōi synechōs āidōn, antēchousēs autōi tēs phōnēs, enomisen auton euphōnon sphodra einai.
sentences.l: A singer to the lyre, without gift, singing constantly in a plastered room, his voice echoing back to him, supposed that he was exceedingly fine of voice.
sentences.i: A singer to the lyre who had no gift for it used to sing constantly in a plastered room, and, since his voice came echoing back at him, took himself for a man of splendid voice.
sentences.n: A κιθαρῳδός sings to his own cithara — a performer's trade, competed at festivals. ἀφυής is "without natural gift", the exact opposite of εὐφυής. A room finished in κονία, lime plaster, rings; the resonance is what flatters him. ἀντηχούσης … τῆς φωνῆς is a genitive absolute giving the cause. νομίζω takes accusative and infinitive.

sentences.t: Καὶ δὴ ἐπαρθεὶς ἐπὶ τούτῳ ἔγνω δεῖν καὶ εἰς θέατρον εἰσελθεῖν.
sentences.tr: Kai dē epartheis epi toutōi egnō dein kai eis theatron eiselthein.
sentences.l: And indeed, lifted up at this, he decided that he must go into a theatre as well.
sentences.n: ἐπαρθείς is the aorist passive of ἐπαίρω, "raised up, elated", and ἐπί with the dative gives the ground of the feeling. ἔγνω, aorist of γιγνώσκω, is here "resolved"; δεῖν inside it is the infinitive of impersonal δεῖ, "that it was necessary".

sentences.t: Ἀφικόμενος δὲ ἐπὶ σκήνην καὶ πάνυ κακῶς ᾄδων λίθοις βαλλόμενος ἐξηλάθη.
sentences.tr: Aphikomenos de epi skēnēn kai pany kakōs āidōn lithois ballomenos exēlathē.
sentences.l: But having come onto a stage and singing very badly, pelted with stones, he was driven out.
sentences.i: But when he came out onto a stage and sang very badly indeed, he was pelted with stones and driven out.
sentences.n: λίθοις is a dative of instrument with the passive βαλλόμενος. ἐξηλάθη is the aorist passive of ἐξελαύνω, "drive out". Chambry prints σκήνην with the accent drawn back to the first syllable, where the accusative of σκηνή is normally σκηνήν; the page is followed as it stands.

sentences.t: Οὕτως καὶ τῶν ῥητόρων ἔνιοι ἐν σχολαῖς εἶναί τινες δοκοῦντες, ὅταν ἐπὶ τὰς πολιτείας ἀφίκωνται, οὐδενὸς ἄξιοι εὑρίσκονται.
sentences.tr: Houtōs kai tōn rhētorōn enioi en scholais einai tines dokountes, hotan epi tas politeias aphikōntai, oudenos axioi heuriskontai.
sentences.l: So too some of the orators, seeming in the schools to be somebodies, whenever they come to public affairs, are found to be worth nothing.
sentences.i: So too, some among the orators who pass in the lecture-rooms for men of consequence are found worth nothing at all once they come to public life.
sentences.n: τινες here is the emphatic indefinite — "somebodies", men of consequence. σχολή is the lecture-room where rhetoric was taught; the πολιτεῖαι are the affairs of the city, where the speaking has to work. ὅταν with the aorist subjunctive is the indefinite "whenever". οὐδενὸς ἄξιοι is a genitive of value.
